utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to -- good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, may we -- could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Douglas Stringer, with Sarah Clanton and Thomas Laugel and intern Mr. Vros Zigic for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. We had intended and forget to mention ahead of time that there was -- there were two preliminaries matters with respect to this witness that we wish to raise or Ms. Clanton needs to raise before the witness is brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We need to go into private session for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: For the second one, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start with the first one then.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. And as was in a proofing note that I provided yesterday, and I would like to notify the Court that in the course of reviewing the Mrksic transcripts of this witness, we discovered that there was a mistake in the interpretation into the English version of an answer he gave in his Mrksic testimony. We were able to review the B/C/S audio with the witness and also with our language staff and confirmed that there is a mistake in the English interpretation. This is part of his 92 ter statement, his Mrksic testimony, and therefore we provided the parties with the information on what he actually said in B/C/S as well as a corrected English translation. If you would like, I can refer to the precise page and line number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. And -- and in -- in the 92 -- sorry. Is it now corrected in the 92 ter statement that we have --

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a testimony. And we have to I think speak further to the Registry about how to correct the official English translation, the official transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's what I was wondering about. You're saying you provided it to the parties, but how -- how would it get to us?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we provided a proofing note we wanted to raise this a preliminary matter and to note that there is problem with the English. This is not something that the witness can really comment on because he doesn't speak English. It's something that we discovered through the course of proofing and were able to confirm that the mistake is simply to do with the interpretation at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Anything from the Defence on --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. So then we go into that private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Witness, can you tell us your name and date of birth and your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragutin Berghofer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 29th of October, 1940. Born in the town of Osijek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And your ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commitment themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out to you that you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give misleading or untruthful evidence to this Tribunal. Can I now ask you to read the solemn declaration the usher will give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You maybe be seated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Berghofer.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Did you testify here in The Hague in March 2006 in the case against Mile Mrksic, Veselin Sljivancanin, and Miroslav Radic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And since you arrived here in The Hague, have you listened to the audio recording of your testimony in that case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And did you recognise that audio recording as your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions today that you were asked at that time, would you provide the same answers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now that you've taken the solemn declaration, do you affirm the accuracy and truthfulness of your audio -- or your testimony in the Mrksic case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, the Prosecution would tender 65 ter numbers 04458, 04459, and 04460 into evidence under seal. These are at tabs 1 to 3. We'd also seek to tender the associated exhibits which are at tabs 4 through 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I probably missed something. Could you tell us why it should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, in the prior proceedings, part of his evidence was given in private session due to the nature of the discussion. We will be providing the Court with a public redacted version of his testimony shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 4460 shall be assigned Exhibit P1065 under seal. 65 ter document 4459 shall be assigned Exhibit P1066.1065, under seal. 65 ter document 4458 shall be assigned Exhibit P1067.1065, admitted under seal. 65 ter document 2828 shall be assigned Exhibit P1068.1065. 65 ter document 2643 shall be assigned Exhibit P1069.1065. 65 ter document 2640 shall be assigned Exhibit P1070.1065. 65 ter document 2644 shall be assigned Exhibit P1071.1065. 65 ter document 3038 shall be assigned Exhibit P1072.1065. And 65 ter document 2645 shall be assigned Exhibit P1073.1065. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: First, Mr. Berghofer, I want to tell you that today when I refer to your evidence in the Mrksic case from 2006, I will refer to it as your Mrksic testimony. I will not say each time the names of the other two persons, Mrksic, Sljivancanin, and Radic, simply because it's easier to refer to it as the Mrksic testimony. In addition, I will be providing page numbers to the English translation of your testimony. You do not need to follow anything on paper, but please just listen to the questions. And as the Chamber has admitted your Mrksic testimony, I'm only going to ask you questions today on a small number of topics. First, I want to ask you about the testimony that you gave in Mrksic about the buses that took you to the JNA barracks on the 20th of November, 1991. In the Mrksic case, when you gave evidence - and this is at transcript page 5280 - you gave evidence that on 20th of November, 1991, you left the hospital in Vukovar in a convoy of six buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Laugel to please play a clip from 65 ter 4986. This has ERN V000-6801. This is at tab 12. We've prepared a clip from the longer video and the 65 ter number of the clip is 04986.1. The relevant time code is from 1 hour, 38 minutes, and 50 seconds, to 1 hour, 39 minutes and 39 seconds. We're not asking that the audio of this video be played or tendered at this time. It's only for the images. And I would first like to ask Mr. Laugel to play the video and pause at approximately 2 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: For the record, we have paused at 1 hour, 38 minutes, 54 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, do you recognise the bus in this still image?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. Those are those buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And when you say "those buses," can you tell me where you've seen this bus before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: They were standing in front of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And do you recognise the bridge that this bus is crossing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. That is the so-called wooden bridge, although it was not made of wood, but that's what people have been calling it for the past 50 years or so. The wooden bridge, "drveni most."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what is the name of the river that is underneath the bridge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Vuka.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And who was on this bus?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I was. And all of those who were at the hospital, as prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: So where was this bus coming from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: From the direction of the hospital, moving towards Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Was it mostly men or women on the bus?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was only one woman in the bus with her son, and that is Dragica Tuskan.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask Mr. Laugel to play a bit more. Please keep your attention focussed on the left-hand side of the screen. And I would like to ask Mr. Laugel to pause at 1 hour, 39 minutes, and 2 seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, what do you see entering the screen in this still image?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, I see Dr. Bosanac; I think that's her.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, if you could please look at the picture that's on the left half of your screen, and I'd like to ask you if you see -- what you see entering the picture on the left half of your screen.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: By the bus, on the left-hand side - I mean, on this left-hand picture - it seems as if the next bus is entering, getting into the picture, on the right-hand side. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And do you know where the second bus was coming from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: One following the other. If I was in the fourth bus, then these three were in front of me, and two behind me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, where was the place that the bus went?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, you see, it's the centre of town. And then we were moving on, say, another 400, 500 metres straight, and then they turned to the right. That is the road to Negoslavci and the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'd like to play to the end of the clip, which is 1 hour, 39 minutes, 39 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, again, Mr. Berghofer, when the screen splits, please focus your attention on the left side of the screen.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Buses are moving.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, I've asked our Case Manager to bring the image back up. Just one moment, please. Mr. Berghofer, who is the taller man standing towards the left of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: That is Major Veselin Sljivancanin. But, of course, I recognised him once I had been released, when I was in Zagreb, when I was watching TV. That's the man who was in command at the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, where is Major Sljivancanin standing when this footage is being taken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: It is -- well, the people of Vukovar call it the newer bridge, but it's actually the wooden bridge is newer than this one. But this bridge in the centre of town was built before the wooden bridge. Say, that is 300 kilometres away. They are 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 300 metres apart in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, can you identify, provide the name of the bridge that is visible in the left portion of this shot? Behind Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, we, the people of Vukovar, since that really used to be a wooden bridge, that was the only bridge that we crossed after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, if you were standing on this new bridge, the one that you just described where Sljivancanin is standing, would you be able to see the wooden bridge?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, you can see it. I told you, it's roughly 300 metres. Maybe it's not even 300 metres. You can see a person normally. You can see anyone you know well. I mean, I cannot say just anyone, but if you know someone well you can see them, recognise them, and also you can communicate with them. You can shout from one bridge to the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And in this video-clip, who is Major Sljivancanin speaking to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I personally always called him "Mirovnjak," the peace maker. The Croatian television also played that. And this Sljivancanin almost grabbed him and threw him into the water, but this man made such an effort. Of course, I don't speak English, but then there was a translation, and also you could see the hand gestures, and you know all of that. You know what Veselin Sljivancanin's response was.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, do you know what organisation the person he is speaking to worked for?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I think he was an Englishman. That's what I found out later. But you know what? The Red Cross was in Mitrovica. Then in Vukovar there were different international institutions, UNTAES, and -- but I he was the first one who was in charge of protecting the wounded and civilians. That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, you described a few moments ago that you saw television footage when you were released from prison and that you were then able to recognise the person who you saw in the hospital as Veselin Sljivancanin. Do you believe that this was the footage that you saw when you were released?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, yes. But I saw him after two years, after two and a half years, after I had been set free once I got a television set.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time the Prosecution would like to tender 65 ter 04986.1 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1074. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Berghofer, I would like to ask you a question about what it was like in Vukovar in November 1991. Towards the middle of November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask Mr. Laugel to please play a clip from 65 ter 04799. And this is going to be 04799.2. The ERN is V000-1131. This is listed at tab 10. We have prepared a clip that is approximately a minute and a half long. The relevant time code from the main video is 1 hour, 24 minutes, and 5 seconds, to 1 hour, 25 minutes, and 30 seconds, and the transcripts for this video have been uploaded and released in e-court and are available under that 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "... from all the buildings and from all the flats. I don't feel sorry for myself or the flat, I feel sorry for all the flats... "... and from all the roofs ... "... about those weapons buried behind the shelter, you know... "... behind the shelter ... they also buried the uniforms... "... they burnt in the hospital, all of those who are in the hospital... "... show us where that is. "Behind the shelter there's a door in ... "Hang on a minute, let us calm down so that we can tell these people... "They have probably mined it? "Yes. No, no. "We don't know if they mined it or not. "Pap Tomislav is, you can check this, the biggest criminal ... I don't know whether he's been hit ... in the hospital. "He did not come yesterday ... but now we've heard that yesterday... "Pap Tomislav? "Pap Tomislav, the biggest criminals, Dosan, Molnar, Dane, Korac, Ivan, who insulted me because I'm a Serbian woman... "Go on, who else? "Pedja. "Go on. You name more of the men that you know. "Agan, that Korac, Ivica ... all of the Molnars ... then a man from Zagorje, put civilian clothes on and went to the hospital. "All right. "And there were more civilians who shot at us. "They all changed their clothes. That boy of 17 ... they were firing from our apartments. "Get ready, the Ustashas have come here right from Germany ... where is Europe now?"

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, what town is this being filmed in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: That is at the bridge that we call the new bridge, Novi Most or grand hotel that stands right in front of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And without using their names, can you tell me if you recognise the women who are shown in this video-clip?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, I knew both of them, and I never had any difficulties with them. I believe that I was even on speaking terms with the blonde lady. We would exchange hellos and -- as a craftsman I also had contacts with them. But let's say that I am acquainted with both of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what ethnicity are they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, the blonde one just said that she was of the Orthodox faith and Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And do you see -- can you please tell the Court who they're talking to.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: It's the Vukovar Territorial Defence. They were now telling each other who they had seen so that, on this side, these reservists started speaking about Tomislav Pap as being the brother of that other man. This other individual mentioned Molnar, then still another mentioned Ivica and Dosen. They're all people from Vukovar, locals, reservists who knew these other men that the woman mentioned and named.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, the men that the woman mentioned and whose names you just provided, Tomislav Pap, Molnars, Dosen, what ethnicity were these people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: As far as I know about the Dosens, they were Croats. As for Molnar, I can also claim that he is a Croat. And most probably Tomislav Pap was as well, judging by his name, although that can be no guarantee. There are names that both the Orthodox people and the Croats have. But I'm guessing, since he was Dr. Bosanac's right hand man, that he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, what happened to Tomislav Pap?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I met Tomislav Pap in the hangar at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And did you ever see him after the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Never again.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, we'd like to tender 65 ter 04799.2 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Registrar tells me there is only an English transcript for this clip. No B/C/S. If that's no problem for the Defence --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1075. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a B/C/S transcript, and we will make sure that that is uploaded and released in e-court as soon as possible. It may actually be attached to the English transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Berghofer, I'd like to move to a different subject. I want to ask you about your familiarity with the facility that you identified as Velepromet in the Mrksic case. In the Mrksic case you were shown aerial photographs, this is at transcript page 5309, the Mrksic transcript, and you indicated that you had been taken very briefly to Velepromet on the 20th of November, 1991, and then again on the 21st of November, 1991. The question I want to ask you is: Had you known of this place called Velepromet before those dates?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: But, of course. I was a neighbour, as it were. I lived 500 metres away from Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that when you arrived there on November 20th and on November 21st, 1991, it was familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask Mr. Laugel to play a clip of 65 ter 04798.3. The ERN is V000-1130. This is at the list at tab 11. Your Honours, I prepared a clip which is approximately 40 seconds long, and the relevant time code for the main video is 36 minutes, 54 seconds, to 37 minutes, 28 seconds. We're not asking that the audio of this video be used. I'd simply like to show it for the images. And if Mr. Laugel could play it and first pause at 37 minutes and 5 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, do you recognise the woman who's being shown in this video?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. She is an inhabitant of Vukovar. The mother of Zvonko Ilis [phoen] who I met at Ovcara and who was subsequently killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now I'd like to play a bit more. If Mr. Laugel could please play it and pause 37.08.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, in this still image, do you see anybody that you recognise?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: The man in the middle is Bratso, Wilhelm. To the right, the tall bearded -- moustached man is Plajner.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And just to clarify for the record, is this -- the man with the moustache in the still image at 37:08, this is the person who appears second from the right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: The second man from the right. The -- the man to the right is Ostojic. To the left is also an old inhabitant of Vukovar, but I simply can't remember his last name at present.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, the person you have identified with the moustache, could you please state his name again for the record?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Plajner. He was with me in Mitrovica. He was in charge of the room in Sremska Mitrovica. He was from Mitnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: When you say that he was in charge of the room, does that mean that he was one of the guards or one of the soldiers or one of the inmates?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: He was one of the inmates.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now I'd like for Mr. Laugel to play this clip to the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, do you recognise where this video was taken?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: At Velepromet, on the right-hand side as you enter the compound. It was a storage facility, and you had around 15 of such facilities. They were containers, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'd like to tender 65 ter 04798.3 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1076. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Berghofer, I'd like to leave the topic of Velepromet and move onto another subject. I want to ask you a small number of questions about the persons who you saw in the hangar at Ovcara on the 20th of November, 1991. First, I would like to ask you a few questions about a document, and I would like to ask the Court Officer to please pull up 02640.1. I would also like for the court usher to provide you with a hard copy, please. Mr. Berghofer, do you recognise the handwriting on this document?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And whose handwriting is it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: As far as I know, it's mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, if you could please look at the top of the page and, again, towards the middle on the right and tell me if you recognise the signature on that page.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. It's mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Berghofer, in the Mrksic case, you testified about a similar list. This was at transcript page 5301 to 5303. I'd like to ask you, if you can confirm, that the names that are listed on the left-hand side of the page, from numbers 1 to 30, are the names that you provided when you testified in the Mrksic case.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And now I see on the right-hand side that there are additional names in your handwriting. Can you tell me, where did you see these people who were listed on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I saw them at Ovcara. Some of them were my neighbours and others were my pals, and my peers. There is maybe 50 more of these, but I couldn't remember all the family names.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, when did you add the names to this list?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: The ones on the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, the ones on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: This morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And when you added the names to the list, did you do it from memory?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we'd like to ask that 65 ter 02640.1 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit 1077. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Berghofer, I want to move on from the topic of Ovcara and ask you a few questions about your imprisonment at Sremska Mitrovica. You've already given evidence in the Mrskic proceedings, and we have a limited time today, so I'm only going to ask you a few questions. On what day did you arrive at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: On the 22nd of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And on that day, where did you leave from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: From the Vukovar barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And how did you get from the Vukovar barracks to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: By Cazmatrans bus. It's the big one. And if you're asking about the trip from the barracks to Sremska Mitrovica, it was a red Cazmatrans bus with the Bjelovar licence plates, a long bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And approximately how many people were on this bus with you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: About 17 or 18, as far as I recall. Dr. Sadika boarded the bus in Negoslavci. There was another woman, aged about 45, and -- that's the two of them. I'm not sure about the third one, but there were three women.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, you mentioned that someone boarded in Negoslavci. Was this the only stop on the bus?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. That was the only place where the bus stopped, at Negoslavci. Dr. Sadika and Slobodan Nikolic got on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And were all the passengers on the bus civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: All of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Were there any other people on the bus who were not civilians?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No. The person who was in charge of the journey and then Djuro, who I knew well, was the driver, and then there was this one who was wearing a light green olive suit of sorts. It could be a dress suit and not necessarily a military uniform. I'm sorry, so this last one, I'm talking about, he was in charge of that trip.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, did you feel that you were free to get off the bus at any time before arriving at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: There was no possibility whatsoever for you to get out of that bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And in the Mrksic case, you described for the Court getting off the bus and running the gauntlet, and this is at transcript page 5379. I would like to know if prior to getting off the bus if you saw anyone in Sremska Mitrovica area who was from the Vukovar area or the surrounding villages of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: As far as I remember, next to Sremska Mitrovica there was a school or a gym. I saw a great many of our women there, and among them, there was Dusko Ostojic. They were circling round that gym. They were outside.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, to clarify for the record, was Dusko Ostojic a man or a woman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: A man. Dusko Ostojic. The father of the man whom I recognised in the hangar in Vukovar who was standing on the right-hand side with eyeglasses.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And approximately how old was Dusko Ostojic at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: He must have been 65 or 66.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And as I said before, you've testified about the gauntlet and the beatings. I'd like for you to briefly describe for the Court the mistreatment and the injuries you received on the 22nd of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I don't think it will be possible to describe it that way. But let me just say this: Horrible, horrible, horrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Were you injured in these beatings?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, I have difficulties with my leg to this day. It's thrombosis. But I wasn't the only one. They -- there wasn't just one man who was beating us. They were all beating us. But there was this one man, Dusko, he was very much into beating. You couldn't even compare him to a lion. He was beating us even harder than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And after this beating, did you receive medical treatment for your injuries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, there was Gajic who was putting bandages on -- on me. I seemed -- I was all black and blue, like I'd been sun-bathing in the Hawaii days. I was barefoot for four or five months. My knees are no good. I can't watch -- I can't read newspapers. And I cannot bear to watch movies about the war. Well, that's all. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, this person named Gajic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: He was a friend of mine from Mitnica. He was also one of the defenders of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, you described in your Mrksic testimony that a man named Soljic was killed, and this is at transcript page 5380 and 5474. I want to ask you: How was Soljic killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: When we got onto the handball court, we had to take our clothes off. Previously, we had been beaten as we were going through the gauntlet. They forced us to strip ourselves naked. They were beating us, especially Dusko who was savagely beating us, and he must have hit the man pretty hard because he could not be roused again. For instance, I fainted on a couple of occasion but I always came to. This man, Niko Soljic, was not panic-stricken at all. Now, there was this one man who was mocking us together with Dusko, whereas there was this other man who told Dusko, How can you treat them this way? And then they took my shoes away. So all of the four and a half months I spent at Sremska Mitrovica I was bare foot.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: How close were you to this person who died, Niko Soljic, and how far away were you sitting or standing from where he was?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Right next to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that yourself and other people fainted from the beatings. How did you find out that Soljic was dead and it was not just that he had fainted?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, since I would get up during the beatings. But I would like to note that they did not beat the people on the right as much as they beat us. Like this one who attacked me. And then when we were supposed to go upstairs, I was carried, but then this man never got up. So, of course, he froze. That's why Dusko said, Look, this guy had lots of ice-cream to eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, did any person at the prison ever talk to you about Mr. Soljic being killed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Not with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear people talking about Mr. Soljic's killing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I don't know. I know this young man, Ularik, a neighbour, gave a statement. They were related in some way, and he went out there to give some statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what do you mean by giving a statement. What was Ularik asked to do you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, you know how things go. That he fell and died. I don't know what the exact text was that the little guy signed over there. I don't know what they asked him. I know that they took him away once so that he would give some statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: When you say "the little guy," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, there was this little guy in the same room where I was. It was a room 3 by 3. He was like 16 years old. That's why I'm saying this little guy. He lived in Slavija, in that building.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And just to clarify, what is the surname of the person that you referred to as the little guy?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Ularik is his last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And you've said that Ularik was taken and that there was text that he signed and a statement. Can you tell me what that was about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, nothing more than that. It's not that he talked about it. It's not that I listened properly. I didn't really have an opportunity to listen properly because there were 152 of us in the room, or 154.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: When he was taken - and I know that you don't know all the details because the room was very crowded as you say - but when Ularik, this young guy, was taken, and asked to give a statement, what event was this statement about?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, first, the question was, who knew him. And then the young boy said that they were related or that somebody was somebody's godparent, and then I guess he went to their office.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, when you say that the first question was who knew him, who are you referring to when you say "him"?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, the late Soljic, Niko.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And just to clarify what you've just said. Can you confirm that you've told us that the question was asked who was related to the late Niko Soljic and that is why this person named Ularik was giving a statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Berghofer, a few moments ago you, you described the room that you were in. You said it was room 3-3. Can you describe the size of the room and the number of people who were kept there?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I know there were 154 or 152 of us. And they never knew exactly how many there were. And every day they came to count us. They would put us on one side, and then we'd run over to the other side, and then they'd count again. And that room was, well, say, 12 metres, 13 metres by 5 and a half or 6 metres. It's hard to say. It's a big room. There weren't any beds there. We slept there but I could personally could not lie on my back, but also the people who were next to me couldn't either. We were packed like sardines. You know, the fish.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Berghofer, how often were you able to shower at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I am sorry. What do you mean, "shower"? There was water. I should note that. There was central heating. I'd like to note that Sremska Mitrovica was empty as far as that facility was concerned, that camp, prison, whatever. And then it was only once that I went to take a shower. When I came to the room that was 2 by 1 metres, but that was 45 days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, if you remember, can you provide the Court with the names of some of the people who you remember being with you? Just a few.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, I can. There was this Plajner. Well, there was lots of people. Buljan, Zeljko. He was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, was there anyone who you had seen at Ovcara who was with you at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: In that room, yes. There was Cakalic, there was Guncevic, and there was myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Were there any women and children in this room?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No, no. No. Not in our room. No one.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Were there women and children in another room?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. I do apologise. Well, there was this young boy in the room 3 by 3, say, he was like 12 years old. He was there with his father. They did want to send him home, however he didn't want to leave without his father. And there were women there because there was this woman that kept shouting, Daddy, where are you? Come help.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, in your Mrksic testimony you said that Goran Hadzic came one time to the prison and that he said that it was stinking very badly, that there was a very strong stench, and this is at transcript page 5381. I'd like to ask you: What was causing the smell in the room?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: It is true that Mr. Hadzic came to the 3 by 3 room, but it's also true that we stank. I have to state it in such vulgar terms because simply we hadn't had a shower for three months. And also a month and a half after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: When you say "a month and a half after that," do you mean a month and a half -- what month and a half time-period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, I'm calculating it now. From the 22nd of November, say, until the 15th of January. I'm just speaking sort of off the cuff now. It is a -- it is correct. I mean, the first date. But then the second one, was it the 20th or the 15th of February 1992? But then all of a sudden, we could bathe when we were in the 2 by 1 room.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Okay, Mr. Berghofer. I'd like to ask you at about the time that Mr. Hadzic came to the prison, what was the condition of the prisoners in that room.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, you see, they were being taken out for interrogations all the time. There were also younger men. That's why they had to go. Whereas, we got some old uniforms of the former JNA, and we had to wear them. These were trousers and jackets.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, approximately what time, what month, do you believe that Mr. Hadzic came to Sremska Mitrovica? Not an exact date but an approximate date.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: December, the 20th or the 21st. In 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And how did you know that the person who was there was Goran Hadzic? How did you recognise him.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Hadzic knows very well where he had his picture taken. Starting from Plitvice, although he was about 500 kilometres away from his own town, Vukovar. And now we call that bloody Easter, we, the people of Vukovar call it that. And that's when there were pictures of Goran Hadzic all over. And then I also knew him by sight as a younger man. We never exchanged greetings. But I was a guest at Bobota and I think I saw him watching a game or something like that. But that was in passing.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And at the time that he was in the prison, do you know what position he held?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I did not know then. I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And when he was in the prison, how far was he standing from where you were?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Right next to me. Right next to me. So the man came, and we all gathered around and we wanted to hear what he had to say. Can I tell you what he said?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: He came in and, of course, he was wearing a military uniform. Somehow it was different from the other SNB ones. He looked left and right, and he said this: "Why don't you let these people go home?" And after that, he left.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, was there anybody else standing with Mr. Hadzic at this time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: My neighbour, Rajak, as far as I can remember. He wore a sort of captain's uniform. He was a young boy, 26, 27. Very nice uniform, brand new. I think he had the rank of captain. But it's been a long time. It's hard to remember. Young man; however, his house is the fourth house next to mine, so that's how I know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And a moment ago, you've told us what you remember Goran Hadzic saying when he was standing next to you in the Sremska Mitrovica prison. I want to ask you if this was the only time that you ever heard Goran Hadzic talking about prisoners, including those at Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. That's the only thing I heard coming from his mouth. He and I, both of us, living creatures. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, I didn't mean to limit to what you heard him say when he was physically in your presence. Did you ever hear this kind of statement from Hadzic, not necessarily when he was standing next to you as a living creature talking to you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I had already been set free and for a year and that place where those six buses were, when they were leaving the hospital, that's the street that was called Bozidar Adzija or Sapudl, and then this journalist, well, usually it was the Novi Sad television that made an effort to take pictures of us and interview him. And this is what he said, at least that's what it looked like on the picture: "All of those Ustashas should be returned so that the Serb people could try them here in Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, just to clarify, when did you see this footage, this journalist you've described speaking to Hadzic? When did you see this interview?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, let's say, 1993. End of 1992. Let me say it wasn't only I who bought a TV set. I imagine some of my friends also had TV sets so we saw that, but I cannot tell you what date it was. At any rate, he was on TV several times so the Croatian TV kept replaying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, you've just stated, and I'm going to say this quotes, "that --" this is at transcript page 29, line 23: "That all of those Ustashas should be returned so the Serb people could try them here in Vukovar." When you heard this, what did it make you think about what you heard at Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, in Sremska Mitrovica, well, sort of in a friendly way when he saw how miserable we were. How badly we stank. He was among us and he was aware of that, that we were not all war criminals. Not everybody who was in that room was a war criminal. But then there was this other statement when he was his own people, and it wouldn't have been convenient for him to defend some Croats because he is under pressure from his open people, so these are two completely different opinions and two completely different utterances.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. My name is Zoran Zivanovic, and I am Defence counsel for Mr. Hadzic in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Good morning. Pleased to meet you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put a few questions to you in relation to your testimony today. First of all, I would like to draw your attention to this video footage that was shown to you by the Prosecutor. It's page 14 of our transcript. And you had the opportunity of seeing two women and a young man in civilian clothing talking to soldiers, people in JNA uniforms. And they were referring to the names of different persons who had allegedly done some bad things to them. Now, this is what I'd be interested in: Among these people in uniform, did you recognise anyone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I cannot guarantee anything, because you know what? As soon as you put a uniform on, you can no longer recognise a man. And, you know, all of these were young men and they could have been my sons. They were 25 or 27 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, may I conclude that you did not recognise anyone who was wearing JNA uniforms in that footage talking to those two woman and the young man?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No, no. Only those women. Had I been able to watch the footage longer, maybe I could have deciphered some more. But all these are younger people. Well, I certainly know their mothers and fathers; but, as for them, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's another thing I wanted to take a look at. Actually, I'd be interested in hearing whether you had an opportunity of reading the list of missing persons from Vukovar, from the Vukovar Hospital, after you had been released; that is to say, when all of this was over and until you testified later?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Never, until then, except when I was in Belgrade with Mr. Vesko Krstajic. I had to put circles around those of the names who I had recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you that precisely because now when you communicated with the Prosecution, there was that list that you had compiled earlier on and you added a few names to that list, I think five or six names, and I'm simply interested in how that happened. How come you remembered those names after 20 years and even more than 20 years?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, if you knew how vividly I still have them in my mind. I still see their images. But I know Pinter, that's the first one I added. He was a friend of mine for 40 years, I mean born then. Then this Misel. I kept talking about Misel -- I mean, sorry, I kept talking about a French man. But I thought that that was a nickname, "Francuz," frenchman - I know this is not your question - but when Kemo was looking for him. And now as Simunic, Pero, is concerned, I think that he was on that first list way back. And then Jarabak, I remember that name. Stanko Duvnjak was a policeman. Then Vukojevic, Slaven. Then the young Zivkovic. Whereas, this Kacic, he was 15 or 16 years old. They simply grabbed him from his mother because -- in hospital because he was a well-developed boy and they put him on the bus. Believe me, Mr. Zivanovic, there's more of them, but I'm always surprised when I come here. Believe me, I'm never prepared. Now this list that I'm holding in my hands, it's Mr. Moore who forced me. I mean, in two and a half minutes I had to scribble this down, although there is this name -- actually, there is this list I have at home, when I came home, 1991, 1992, when I came from prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing. On page 21 of the transcript today, you said that all the people who were on that bus that went to Sremska Mitrovica, that all of them were civilians. As I read your testimony in the Mrksic case, I note that you said there, among other things, that were in the 204th Brigade, and you also said what battalion, what company you belonged to. So now I'd be interested in hearing in whether there were other people who were in a position that was similar to yours, among the people that you marked as civilians.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, you know what it was like in our situation in Vukovar. Whoever had been in a cellar made sure that he got the status of a defender of Croatia. Ljubo --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the last name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ljubo Pribudic was on the bus and he managed to get that status, and then also Zeljko Buljan, and he had allegedly even been wounded. Sinisa Veber also managed to get that. Although, believe me, when I look at these names here, some of them didn't even bring a glass of water either to one or the other. If nothing else, at least in the beginning I participated at the radio station and then in logistics. And then there are others, too. Vili Karlovic, for instance. He is from Zagreb. He came to help out. He came from Zagreb. He's a participant too, isn't he? Then who else? Let me try to remember now. Guncevic, Stjepan. And you need an automatic rifle to get him to come and testify, but he has the status of a Croatian defender. Whoever survived Vukovar was given the status of a defender of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now could you please clarify this for us. Does that mean that people who were civilians who did not take part in any military units in any way, did they -- or, rather, were they included in the 204th Brigade and its different companies and battalions, or were these people who had been actually deployed in these units but did not take part in direct combat or, rather, were not at the front line where the fighting took place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know even this young boy, Ularik, aged 16, even he was a defender of Vukovar. But let me tell you once again, Mr. Zivanovic, maybe these people, I mean, maybe I underestimated them now and maybe I offended them in some way now. I didn't mean to. But maybe they were also involved, maybe they were engaged by some of their commanders. Maybe they were supposed to bring water at least or food. So there's always some work drive that was under way during the defence of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think this is time for a break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed. Thank you Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Berghofer, we take our first break now. We'll come back at 11.00. The court usher will escort you out of court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, there is Prosecution motion to add missing pages to exhibit numbers 987 to 992. Adding missing pages. Could you give us your position or tell us when you could give us your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No objection. Thank you. Then the motion is granted, as prayed. Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you spoke about the gauntlet that you and the others who got off the bus had to pass through when you arrived in Sremska Mitrovica. Is my understanding correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you didn't know the people who were there, are you able to say what the formation was that they belonged to? Did they wear uniforms? Were they in any way identifiable?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, they had their uniforms as prison guards, as doormen. They were people working for the Sremska Mitrovica prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also spoke of the beatings that the inmates at Sremska Mitrovica suffered. You also mentioned Dusko. Presumably he is from Vukovar. That's where you know him from.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I didn't know a single person there. I wouldn't be able to tell you that it was Dusko had it not been for his friend who, when he saw Dusko beat the other one unconscious and when I fainted, he said to him, "Dusko, how can you act in this way?" And this was only through hearing him say this, Mr. Zivanovic, that I knew that the man was called Dusko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were they also prison guards or were they some other people?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: They were prison guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about the video footage you viewed after your release from prison when you got a TV set and, according to you, it would have been 1992 or 1993. You said that you saw Goran Hadzic being interviewed. You also mentioned that it was close to the place where these six buses were, and my understanding is that this should have been in Vukovar; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have that video footage, but we do have footage which shows roughly what you were talking about. However, the footage was taken in Sid. That's why I'd like to ask you the following: Are you sure that the footage was made in Vukovar and not in Sid, the one you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Zivanovic, we were discussing the street where the buses used to stand, the street next to the hospital, and we used to call it next to "Crvani Magazin." This was roughly 200 metres away from the hospital. It was just that street where buses used to stand back in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, you mean to say that this footage was filmed in that same place where the buses used to stand, although, of course, it was filmed sometime after that event with the buses.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what you heard Mr. Hadzic say, tell us, please, did Goran Hadzic say in that footage, if you remember, that these people who committed crimes should be tried in Vukovar and that, in the second and third instance, they should be tried in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, he didn't say that much. It was just two or three points that he made. He said that these people should be brought back. These Ustashas should be brought back to Vukovar so that the Serbian people can put them on trial. So that's roughly what I heard. But, you know, this was quite a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say this was a few years ago or quite a -- a few, many years ago?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No. Well, I -- it's been a long time. What I wanted to say was that this wasn't the only footage of Mr. Hadzic giving a statement to a team, a TV crew from Serbia or elsewhere. There were a great many other such clips on the Croatian TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether in that same footage Mr. Hadzic said, in addition to what you told us, that it is better to release 100 people who are guilty than convict one innocent man?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is your fifth time testifying before the Tribunal. A couple of days ago, you were able to have a look at your testimony from the Mrksic case. I'm interested in one portion of your evidence in that case where you were put a question and gave an answer. This is Exhibit 4460, pages 67 and 69. This was your testimony on the 3rd of March. You said that nobody from the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia prepared you for testimony; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in relation to your testimony in The Hague - and I don't mean today, I mean previously - did you have any contacts at all with the Ministry of Defence of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: As far as I remember, and I remember well, never. No, not at any point.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the information that we have, your first contact with the OTP and their investigators was in 1994/1995. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was in the Vinkovci police building or whatever you wish to call them. It wasn't something that anybody dared talk about, but I did talk to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that it wasn't something that one was allowed to talk about, do you mean that there was somebody forbidding that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I don't know if it was Mr. Williams or Niemann. Please don't hold me to that. My state had no business interfering with my testimony in The Hague. It was a public secret. I'll tell you that I didn't -- I wasn't allowed to say if I had told these gentlemen anything, because my state did not have the right to put any sort of pressure on me when it came to this Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is my understanding of what you're saying correct: Does this mean that these two persons from the Tribunal told you that you should not be talking about this with people from the Croatian state authorities?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, yes. Roughly along those lines. How can I explain this to you? This was not an issue to be bandied about. It was nobody's business to advise me on this, and if I recall correctly they came back for four visits. They even came to see me at my home, and on their way there was this accident that they had with a tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And in 1996 you gave a statement before this Tribunal here in The Hague for the first time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. Roughly like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, we do have this statement of yours. This is Exhibit 4455. It was given on the 27th of March, 1996. And I suppose you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see on page 17 in e-court of this statement of yours, you said that at one point a high official, a senior official came to the hangar where you were who mistreated some of the prisoners. And you described what it was exactly that he was doing. This isn't important. But you did say that was a high-ranking official. You didn't name him though. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your later testimonies, you claimed that this high-ranking official was Slavko Dokmanovic; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what was the reason why you did not say that it was Slavko Dokmanovic, if you knew that it was him, already back in -- on the 27th of March, 1996?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: In fact, I would need the assistance of -- of the Judge now, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Berghofer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Am I allowed to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You're allowed to speak, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Zivanovic, at the time I was giving the statement, I was told that I should not name the high-ranking official at that point who was seen at Ovcara. Rather, when the cameras were turned off and the journalists stepped out, they came back into the room and said, Mr. Berghofer, who was the high-ranking official whose name you did not say a moment ago? And then I said, Slavko Dokmanovic. And it all took place on that same day, at an interval of 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell who was it who said that you shouldn't name the person, that you should withhold it from the Court?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I think it was the Judge in charge. It was a public hearing, the journalists were present, and I suppose that it was done so that this would not go out into the public domain, that it would remain hidden within the four walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me when was it that, as you said, the Judge in charge told you to proceed that way?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Those who conducted the interview with me knew this. And before I got into the courtroom, they told me that I should not mention him. That's why I referred to him as a high-ranking official from the municipality of Vukovar. And that was the end of that quotation. And then, 30 minutes later, when the room or the hall, whatever you wish to call it, was emptied of journalists and TV people, I gave that testimony that you have in front of you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know, I'm a bit puzzled by your explanation. Normally confidential information is given in closed sessions that would exclude the presence of journalists and the public in general. But this is your explanation.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, that's it. That's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see, this is what I find odd about it. And, please, if you can explain it. On the 27th of March, 1996, the transcript of this statement of yours, page 17, before you gave the statement you took an oath that you would be telling the truth and not withhold any information in response to questions. I wonder now, that after having taken the oath, you adhered to this piece of advice, whoever it was who gave it to you, that this was -- who told you that this was something that shouldn't reach the public and should stay in closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. Mr. Zivanovic what do you read in -- in the oath? What do you read -- read in the oath?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that he was sworn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is the first -- the first page of the -- of this evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Could you read it for me, please, rather than.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the transcript, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's -- it's -- the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's the transcript in the court? It's the transcript of a court session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. But then is there anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is there anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is 4455.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is there anything specific in the oath about not withholding information?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, that's what you're telling the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I -- as far as I know, it is usual for any sworn, for any solemn declaration, or -- or maybe I -- I misunderstood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, the question is -- the question is what a witness can understand when reading that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah. I'll clarify it with him, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell us whether you remember whether you gave a solemn declaration on that occasion, the occasion that I was asking you about. Did you state that you will say the truth? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I remember that, but it wasn't this room. It was a bigger room. And there was glass also. And there were journalists behind me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the declaration? Can you remember the wording of that declaration?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Tell me what declaration you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That you will be telling the truth. Were you asked to take a solemn oath to say that you would speak the truth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. Just like now. But it was only 30 minutes. Help me with this: They had to turn off the TV cameras to be there without journalists. I mean, I'm just there to listen, not to command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did you understand this solemn declaration of yours to tell the truth? Did that mean that if you knew certain information that is important, and that information is that you recognised a man who tortured prisoners there, was your understanding that you were not supposed to say that? Did you think that that would fit into this solemn declaration that you took?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, yes, it does fit in. I don't see the difference between 25 minutes, 30 minutes. I point it out. That's what they told me. Until the cameras went off and until the journalists were no longer there. I mean, how I can explain this to you? I wasn't a secret witness. Things were normal, out in the open. However, in order for the big public not to be reached, well, I told you what happened. A high official from the municipality of Vukovar was there. And, before that, they told me that I should not say that until that happened so that oath of mine, as far as I know, includes both one and the other. Mr. Zivanovic, there's a 30-minute difference. Not six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at 2298. That is number 3 from the Defence list. You see, this is a document of the Ministry of Defence of the Office of the Assistant Minister. And you see your name and surname there as the subject of this document, and it has to do with some information concerning your testimony. Can we take a look at page 2 now. Page 2 of this document. You see what it says here. It says that during 1994 and 1995, there are names of persons who spoke to you, and it says what was discussed on that occasion. It also says -- actually, there's that name, Dokmanovic. It also says what happened in 1996, that you had telephone communication with The Hague. Then the content of this communication. Details of your departure and so on. So I'd like to know whether you provided the Ministry of Defence with this information.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No, no. Look, I was surprised when I saw this. Something similar. And I thought that, to this day, my state did not know that I was in The Hague because I did not contact anyone. It was only with your colleagues from Belgrade that I had to go to Zagreb, I think three times, or twice, where I said the same thing about Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic. So I mean, I didn't understand you. I didn't understand you. I mean, had you told me, telephone, Zagreb, The Hague, I mean, I never had anything to do with that. I just repeat who was with us at Ovcara, who beat us, if I recognised that, and then I have been saying one and the same thing all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move onto the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see here it says that you were heard on the 28th of March and that before you entered the courtroom, names are mentioned here, some names have been crossed out, and you were told that during the first part of your questioning you should not mention the name of Slavko Dokmanovic because journalists were present. That is precisely what you have been telling us now. Tell us whether you conveyed this information to the Ministry of Defence of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: No. Because there are some things here that are not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Well, look what it says here. Cakalic until he fainted. After an hour, Berghofer, along with eight other men was taken away from Ovcara, whereas others were thought to be in a position to commit suicide. He mentioned Emil Cakalic and Guncevic, Stjepan, who is at the blue lagoon, "Plava Laguna." Well, look, it's true. We know all the time -- we've always known who survived Ovcara. I don't know where you got this and I don't know where the gentleman from The Hague got this. I mean, I really don't know. But, look, I co-operate with them. Mr. Williams, it says here, well, yes, I gave statements, and I noted that the gentlemen came to Vinkovci about three times while I was a displaced person, and then they allegedly came to Osijek from the Tribunal in The Hague, from their office, I don't know how to put this. So there are many things here that I do not think are in dispute at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We're going to look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the next document -- or, rather, it is document 2232. It's the next document on our list. That's not the document. That's for sure. 2322; I beg your pardon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is also a letter that the Ministry of Defence sent to President Tudjman in 1998. And it refers to the activities that were taken with a view to protecting the interests of the Republic of Croatia before the International Criminal Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Excuse me, could you please direct me to where this is on the Defence list?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is document number 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: On the list that I see, that's 65 ter 1535 which I believe is a different document. Perhaps the Registrar can tell me if I'm incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I have not updated list, but it must be on our list. 2322.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see the document on the Defence list that was sent through at the beginning of the cross. I just want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I -- for myself, I'm trying to find the Defence list, and I don't find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So it is not on this list, Mr. Zivanovic [Microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Not at the last list, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Not at the last list, a previous one?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry. Not at this last one, at a previous one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It is -- it is an error in -- from our part. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: This is a 35-page document that we haven't seen on any list, and I would ask that we have the opportunity to look at it before he is able to ask the witness about it because it should have been notified to us at the beginning of his testimony this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would after the break be okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No -- I would just say that I would refer just to one sentence of this document, not a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
