utterances.text: I think it would be more appropriate for us to be able to see the context of the one sentence. Having not seen the document, I would like to review it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would after the break be okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Would you wait with your question until after the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- break --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: However, it is the last issue on -- in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's the last issue in your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Which would take how long? Just a few minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Five minutes. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And then what do we expect for re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to consult with my colleagues. I don't think we would have much, if anything, on re-direct. I would still, though, like the opportunity to look at the document even if it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Shall we take a half an hour break now then and come back for that last question of -- or, no. I first -- I should ask first do we have another witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. The next witness is here and ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My microphone is not activated. Mr. President, I'm informed that the next witness is here and she's ready, and so if we could take the half-hour break now, I'd suggest we could come back and take the last few minutes to complete the witness and then continue with the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll take the break. Mr. Witness, we'll take an early break, come back at 12.10. The court usher will escort you out of court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Clanton, while we're waiting for the witness, the translation problem you mentioned in the -- in the proofing note. We don't have that on the record yet; right? I mean, the -- the -- the right translation? How -- how can we have that on the record? Eventually by tendering the proofing note, but I don't know whether the Defence will object to that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Mr. Stringer would like to address you on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, what we could propose to do is if the Defence is in agreement about the correction that needs to be made, because we've indicated precisely what that is, and we can -- perhaps they can listen to the audio, if they would like to do so themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If the Defence is in agreement, then perhaps we could read into the record now, or today, or tomorrow, what the parties believe the correction needs to be. Ultimately because it's an official transcript from a different trial and the transcript from the other trial will have to be corrected by CLSS, so that once the translation is -- or the transcript is officially corrected, then we can, perhaps, substitute the corrected transcript for the one that's now in evidence, and for the -- in the meantime, until that takes place, if the parties are in agreement as to the language at issue, that could be read into the record, just as a way to put it as a placeholder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I understand you to say, Mr. Stringer, that, basically, the issue isn't ready yet to be read into or, whatever, into the record to be on the record. You still need -- or the Defence needs time to check your -- your translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. We haven't heard from the Defence, and I don't even know -- we could -- we could provide them with the audio now, but I don't know that they've had a chance to listen to the audio or to the particular segment yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We could check it this afternoon, or tomorrow, and got back to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's good. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I failed to introduce a member of our team, Ms. Lea Bataillard, who joined us meanwhile. And, also, I would tender the document used with the witness. It is from our list, 2298.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit D31. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I will now show you another document by the Ministry of Defence. That's 2322. Dated the 4th of June, 1998. It's a report by the Ministry of Defence addressed to the president, Franjo Tudjman, as you will see, about the activities undertaken by the ministry in order to protect the interests of the Republic of Croatia vis-a-vis the ICTY in The Hague. We will look at one short portion of the report. This is paragraph 5 at page 14 in the B/C/S version, which is page 22 in the English version. Right at the top of the page is paragraph 5, that's in the B/C/S version, which reads that: "The service participated in the preparation of Prosecution witnesses in the event that the indictment against Mrksic, Radic, and Sljivancanin would be confirmed and in the trial against Dokmanovic, (Vilim Karlovic, D Berghofer, Marin Vidic, aka Bili)." I will go back to the question that I put to you once already. Before the 4th of June, 1998, did you have any contacts with the Ministry of Defence and did it prepare you for your testimonies in these two cases?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, Mr. Zivanovic, no, never. I had never been together with Vilim Karlovic and Marin Vidic, Bili.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the last names that you mentioned. Now it is all right. You see, it was not my understanding on the basis of this text that you were all at the Ministry of Defence at the same time. Rather, what they say here is that they participated in the preparation of Prosecution witnesses. They named the three of you, which does not mean to say that all three of you weren't present there at the same time. They could have been working with each of you separately.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Should I answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Thank you. See, not even my surname is properly spelled here. My assumption is that some of them referred to my name as well. From what I remember, the Ministry of Defence does not even know that I'm alive. Who -- what would I be -- why would I be of any importance to Zagreb? So I really don't know what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In that case, I thank you for your answers. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Only first page of this document and the paragraph 5 of -- 5 of the same document. Not whole document.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Clanton.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I believe that Defence counsel has used the document and in the record it shows that he has asked him a question about that one line, which has been asked and answered. I don't believe that the foundation has been laid to admit this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In our submission it is impeachment material. It is very relevant for assessment of witness -- witness testimony and evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness has confirmed that he never seen the document and he doesn't know anything about it. He was asked about the one proposition, and he answered a question about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, rather than impose on you to file a new and -- new document, we think that everything you want to tender is on the record, so we don't need the document anymore. So we will not admit -- yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that case, I withdraw my -- my request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you finished your cross-examination, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Clanton, re-direct?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, earlier today Defence counsel asked you questions about a hearing that you participated in in 1996, in March of 1996. This was a hearing what was held in The Hague, and you described for the Chamber that when you came for this hearing, you testified, and it was in public and that there were reporters there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: You mean for this Tribunal here? In 1996?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Yes. At this Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: In relation to Slavko Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: In March of 1996, when you came here for this hearing that Defence counsel asked you about and you said that there was a senior Serb official present in the hangar in Ovcara. Do you recall, as you've stated, I want to make sure that you remember that this was a public hearing and that there were reporters there for the first part of it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, it was public. The room was big, but that the Defence counsel asked me that, that's something I can't remember. I only remember that I got from the person in charge in transmission that I should proceed that way. Do you know how it was that Mr. Klein caught Dokmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, when that hearing ended, did the reporters leave?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. And the cameras were switched off. That's what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Okay. And, Mr. Berghofer, do you remember that on that day - that would have been the 27th of March, 1996 - that you received any news about your family in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And what news did you receive about your family in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: My wife's husband died.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Wife's father died, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, did you receive that information when you were here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, right here. I was told by the presiding officers, officer, I'm sorry, you know, apologising for the fact that that's how things were and expressing sympathy.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, this Presiding Judge or officer who expresses sympathy to you, was this when you came back for the closed session hearing?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's how it happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And do you remember that the Presiding Judge in that case said to you that because of the terrible circumstances facing your family and this being a very difficult time, that the Tribunal would like to hear immediately from you and that way, without delay, you could get on a plane and return to your family in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: If that is correct, when I came back to give that other statement 30 minutes later, there wasn't much more that I could say. I was done in a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, when you came back for this hearing, this discussion with the Judges and the Prosecutor that took place 30 minutes afterwards, is that when you answered the questions about Slavko Dokmanovic and provided his name to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes. But, Your Honours, at the time, I didn't already know. Actually, I think it was the very moment that I learnt that the person died. So it all happened in the space of one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Berghofer, when you came back to the Tribunal in 1998, do you remember being present in the case of Slavko Dokmanovic in February 1998 and giving evidence in that case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: And, at that time, did you answer all of the questions that you were asked accurately and truthfully?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: I did. And I even saw him.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: You saw him in the courtroom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Mr. Berghofer, I'm going to change subjects. In your cross-examination Defence counsel has asked you about meetings or discussions or sharing of information with the Croatian services, including the Ministry of Defence, and you've been given a chance to see two documents that have your name in them. What I want to ask you is that every time that you've testified before this Tribunal, have you testified based on your memory accurately and truthfully?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Have you ever been asked by the authorities in Croatia, including in the Ministry of Defence, to give them information about what you knew about Ovcara in order that they would have that related to your testimony at The Hague?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: Only in Zagreb, at a court when the gentlemen from Belgrade came and I had to give a statement similar to the one I gave here. Also when I attended individual hearings about certain specific war crimes, which took place in Vukovar, but that didn't have to do with Ovcara. As far as Ovcara is concerned, I know that nobody ever asked me anything about it because they don't know the exact number that was there, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I want to ask you to pause there. These proceedings that you mentioned in Zagreb and Belgrade, these are local proceedings, and in those proceedings you did not interact with anybody from the ICTY, the Prosecutors or the Judges; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGUTIN BERGHOFER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Berghofer, this brings your testimony before the Tribunal to an end. You are now released as a witness. We thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal, and we wish you a safe journey home. The court usher will escort you out of court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CLANTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have just a moment to switch places, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Witness. Do you understand me in a language -- do you hear me - sorry - in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us your first name and name, date of birth, and ethnicity, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Samira Baranjek, 21st of February, 1966, in Vukovar, Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to give the solemn declaration by which witnesses compel themselves to tell the truth. I point out to you that by doing so, you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give untruthful information to the Tribunal. Can I ask you to read now the solemn declaration the usher will give you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Rachel Friedman for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Your witness, Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Baranjek.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Where did you live in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: In Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And were you married at the time?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: What was the name of your husband?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Ivan Baranjek.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you and your husband have children?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And what are their names?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Tamara and Ivana Fransiska.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: How old were your daughters in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Tamara was 7; and Ivana Fransiska was six months old.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Were you employed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Was your husband employed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. My husband worked at the city -- Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: What was his job there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Nurse.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And other than working as a nurse, how else would your husband spend his time?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Well, he painted. He was a poet. Also did sculpture. Published two books.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Croat. Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you or your husband know Goran Hadzic before the war?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: I just knew him by sight, but my husband knew him a bit better.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: How did your husband meet him?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Well, he came to the hospital, Hadzic, and my husband worked at the TVC department, and he was asking for help for someone close to him, I don't know who it was, who was a patient at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak into the microphone? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, did you hear the comment? The interpreters would like you to move a little bit closer to the microphone so that we can hear you better.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And after this first acquaintance between your husband and Goran Hadzic, do you remember, first of all, approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. When your husband and Goran Hadzic met at the Vukovar Hospital, do you remember what year that was or approximately what year?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: 1988 or 1989, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And after that first meeting, did they continue to have contact?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can you describe what was -- how they interacted.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Well, my husband read poetry on Radio Vukovar, the then-Radio Vukovar. Mr. Hadzic was also involved in poetry. He actually wrote poetry, and he wanted his poetry to be read as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And was your husband -- did your husband help him in any way have his poetry read?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. It went through the director of Radio Vukovar; my husband was on good terms with him. So then some of his poetry was read there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did you ever have a chance to see Goran Hadzic during this time that he knew your husband?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Well, I saw him a few times because in the house where we lived, my husband had a studio, and Mr. Hadzic came a few times to his studio and that's where they looked at paintings, read poetry.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can you say -- well, was it a few times that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, three or four times.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did your husband tell you anything about Hadzic, like where he was from or what job he had?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. He said to me that he worked at some warehouse in Pacetin.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, did the escalation of the conflict cause you at any point to leave your home?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: In October 1991, when Vukovar was bombed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Then I went to the Vukovar Hospital, together with my husband and children. Actually, my husband worked at the hospital, and I went to the shelter there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: How long were you at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Well, about 15 days. Fifteen days at the shelter in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Then my husband was in charge of the wounded. They took them to Komerc, Borovo, and then I went there with my children because there was a shelter there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And what did you do while you were in the shelter?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Well, I took care of my children. I visited the wounded and helped as much as I could. My husband did his job.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: How many people were taking shelter in that location?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: In Borovo Komerc, there were a lot of people. I could not give you the exact number, but there were a lot of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And other than Borovo Komerc, were there other locations nearby where people were taking shelter?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, within the factory itself. That's where people also sought shelter.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I will now ask Mr. Laugel to play a clip from 65 ter 4789.2. The time code is 23:18 to 25:55, and it's at tab 4. I will ask Mr. Laugel to begin playing the clip at 25:20 and pause at 25:36.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: "Overnight, the army had closed off the northern part of Vukovar where the hospital lies. Better delay the evacuation. The Red Cross convoy was turned around, and their delegate didn't like it. "We got used to better collaboration from the JNA before yesterday than I'm getting today. "He found the army commander unsympathetic. "You're not welcome if you don't ... and his soldiers were killed this night also. It's war here. "The war that had destroyed the town had recked the hospital and for today's operation the army was in charge. The major moved out the 300 civilians, mostly Croatians, who'd sheltered in the hospital grounds. They were the first to leave. But the main part of the operation was the transfer of 420 hospital patients, most of them stretcher cases, which sheltered in the basement under fire and under siege for two months. Also, ten mothers and their newborn babies born in appalling conditions. The evacuation has hindered by the suspicion not just between Serbs and Croat but between the federal army and the International Red Cross. The Red Cross protested again. "As you may notice, the International Committee of the Red Cross is completely unable to perform the task that was entrusted to it by the parties. "The major rejected the protest out of hand: The Red Cross, he said, was walking around town trying to control the units of the Yugoslav Army. "And there was another setback for the hospital staff, the real heroes and heroines of Vukovar, when their patients had to wait for hours before the destination was known. The main road to Croatia was blocked by heavy fighting. Instead the convoy headed east to a hospital in Serbia, where the wounded will spend the night."

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we -- this is actually the point where I intended to start, but we let it go for that minute and a half or so since it is relevant to the trial and not too long. But I'm just going ask Mr. Laugel to continue playing the clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: "And at a factory near Vukovar where the Croats had held out till the last, the army was rounding up a thousand civilians and 500 former soldiers. There is a massive and forced migration of people going on."

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. And now I'll -- I'll now just ask Mr. Laugel to play a still from what we just saw at 25:20 so that we can have the witness's comment on that. Sorry, 25:36.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: "The army was rounding up a thousand civilians and 500 former..."

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: In any event, I apologise for the technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Baranjek, in the location that we saw in the second part of the clip, did you recognise that location and did you recognise any of the people?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And just for the record, that time code 24:25.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Sorry, Ms. Baranjek.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, Mrs. Katica, who was with us at Komerc, and then she went to the Borovo factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So the location that we saw, the building that we saw, did you recognise that building?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: That's Borovo Naselje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And do you know when it was that the people came out of the shelter as was depicted in the video?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: The 19th of November, 1991. It was during the morning hours, up to midday. From the Borovo factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And do you know where they were taken from there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: I don't know about them. I don't know where the buses went. I know from what the lady knew that they went to Velepromet Vukovar, but I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Which lady are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Mrs. Katica, the one I mentioned a moment ago, the one wearing a red coat that is here in this footage.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 4789.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1078. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And, Ms. Baranjek, did those of you in the Borovo Komerc shelter surrender as well?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. But we got out of Komerc only later in the afternoon, around 4.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And what led you to come out of Komerc around 4.30?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes. 4 --

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: 1630. Komerc had been bombed. They were throwing tear gas, it was on fire, and we had to go out. Before that, the army was calling out to us to get out. This started from the early morning hours, they were using loud-speakers.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And when you went outside, what type of armed forces did you see, if you were able to recognise them?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. It was the regular army, the JNA, mostly younger soldiers. And behind the Komerc fence further down there were paramilitary forces in civilian clothing, in uniform, camouflage, armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And what did they do when you came out?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: The army or?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Yes, the army.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Nothing. The army people told us to stand in a column. First, the women and children got out, and after that, they carried out the wounded. So we were all standing in a column. And the JNA didn't do anything bad to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: How long were you standing in that column?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Well, for an hour and even longer. Until the buses arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Were you taken anywhere from there by bus?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No. From there, we had to go on foot because the paramilitary forces that were there and these armed men in front did not allow the buses to get through, so then we had to walk along the road 3 kilometres, perhaps even more than that, to Trpinska Cesta, in a column.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: At Trpinska Cesta, did you then board the buses?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. That's where we boarded the buses.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: How many buses were there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a few columns of buses and trucks. I boarded the third bus, if you look it from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Where did that bus take you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: They drove us along from Trpinska Cesta, through the village of Vere, across fields into Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Were there any other vehicles escorting the buses?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. At the very head of the column, there was a military vehicle. It was called a Pinzgauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And where did the buses ultimately arrive?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: They arrived in front of the elementary school in Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you observe anything about the area outside and around the school?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. Opposite the school, there is a sports ground now -- or, rather, when we arrived there, there was a big bulldozer there. Probably there was something that was being worked on there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did -- were you together with your family on the bus?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. I, my husband, and the children.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened when you got off the bus.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Well, when we got off the bus, a policeman from the time met my husband, and he knew him, but he started beating him. And he ordered me to go into the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did the man -- sorry. When you arrived in the elementary school, was that then on the evening of November 19th?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. It was already dark by then.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And before we get into the details, can you just tell us when you eventually left the school? How long were you in the school?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: All night. And I left the school only the next evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: When you arrived in the school, was anything taken from you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. In front of the school, there were men, women; the local population. They were spitting at us. They were taking away our bags, looking for weapons purportedly. They took off the jewellery that we were wearing. They took it off us. And they took our other valuables.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And once you got into the building, were you free to move around?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: What type of forces were in the building then? What type of people were controlling what you did?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a few local people there who lived in the village, and there were people from elsewhere. People that I didn't know. But they all had some kind of uniforms. Also, there were caps with cockades. Different ones. With weapons ...

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you see Goran Hadzic in the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. He came afterwards, when I was still standing in the hallway waiting to be registered.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And where exactly did you observe him? You were in the hallway. Where was he?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: He passed through the hallway and entered the gym of that school.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did you see or hear him do anything in the gym?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. When he walked in, he had actually walked in with some of his people. He was shouting. He was ordering them to do something. He asked who various people were. He entered the gym. Some people were already introducing themselves. They were basically being interrogated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you hear him say anything specific that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. When he entered the gym, he said that everybody would be questioned and whoever is not guilty would be allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did he himself question anybody?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he was questioning anybody because I didn't hear that, but he was inside and he was looking for some people. He asked, there were two people in white coats, and he said, Is Baranjek there as well? That what is what I did hear. I heard that myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you hear any response to the question whether Baranjek was there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And, at this time, did you -- were you able to see or hear where your husband was?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that he was in the gym. And I also heard his voice when he was introducing himself, but I couldn't see him, because I was standing on the side.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did you hear Hadzic say anything to the men who had brought you to the school?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. That's a leading question. There's nothing to establish that he said anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Friedman.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Well, the question is just whether she testified to what he said to the people who were being held in the gym, and I was asking whether he said anything to those who brought them into the gym.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What's been suggested in the question is that Hadzic said anything to this individual. That's suggestive.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I could phrase the question as what, if anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: What, if anything, did Hadzic say to the people that brought you into the school.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: The police - that was then called milicija - that entered the premises, at the point Mr. Hadzic was shouting at them, telling them to go out and not to interfere in his work.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time that you moved somewhere else -- that you were taken somewhere else in the building?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. A lady came, and since I was standing on the side with my children, she took me to a smaller room where otherwise the janitors had a small room of their own where they'd ring the school bell. There was a table there, two or three chairs, and there were radio transmitters on the school desks in there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And what were -- what happened in that room?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: The lady put down my name, the names of the children, my ethnicity. She wrote down my particulars.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did anybody else come into the room?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic came into the room later. He entered briskly arrogantly. He asked me, Where is your husband? He took the radio transmitter, the radio set - what's it called? - to talk.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did he talk into the radio set?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, he was shouting, laughing. He was shouting euphorically, "Belgrade, Mladjo, send reservists over. Vukovar has fallen. I can head for Osijek tomorrow."

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I will now ask Mr. Laugel to play a video-clip, 65 ter 4896.1. The time code for this clip is 23:29 to 24:03 and it's at tab 13. And I will ask to ask to play from the beginning and then to pause for a moment at time code 23:37.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, this isn't an objection. There was a name mentioned, I believe, by the witness, is not reflected in the transcript. It pertains to the alleged conversation or speaking into the radio transmitter.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: So before we play the clip, Ms. Baranjek, did you hear when Mr. Hadzic was speaking into the radio, you mentioned a particular person that he was speaking to. Can you repeat that name, please.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Mladjo.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "It happened four days ago when we were liberating Borovo Selo [as interpreted], my units."

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Baranjek, do you recognise the person that's seen in the video?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: It's Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: He mentioned the location Borovo Naselje. Where is that location?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. The building can be seen a bit. There is a residential building in the background, but where exactly it is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, he says he's speaking about liberating Borovo Naselje, and I just wanted to know whether any of the buildings that you've mentioned today are located in the vicinity of Borovo Naselje?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, it's Borovo Naselje. The column that was in front of the factory, all of that is Borovo Naselje.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And can we now play the rest of the clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Is it a serious wound? "No, it's a light wound, and I returned to the front line immediately, so I have not been absent from the front line at all. "There is a hole in the gun as well. "Yes, this is a hole. This is how it was, there is a hole. This is a small-calibre sniper. It's over and forgotten now. "What next? "Well, we go on. We go to Osijek, Osijek."

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And Your Honours, we tender this 65 ter 4896.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1079. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Ms. Baranjek, returning now to Hadzic's presence in the room with the radio communication, was there anything else that you he heard him say while he was there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. He asked the lady who was writing my particulars down, who was registering me, how many doctors were there in the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did she respond to him?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. She said that there was Dr. Remedi and Dr. Matic-Kutuzovic who needed transportation for Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And was there any other conversation between them?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No. Again, he called on the radio set and said, "Braco, send cars over. There are no cars in the village."

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And what happened after that? Did you remain in this room?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No. The lady took me out, together with the children. We passed a corridor and stepped into a classroom where there were already women and children. There were about 20 of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Was anybody guarding the room?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. There was a guard in front of the classroom. We were in the classroom, and he would lock the door.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did anybody go in and out of the room during the night?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Can you repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did anybody go in and out of the room during the night.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. This same lady came into the room and brought some milk for the children. Mr. Hadzic also entered the room.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Can you describe what he did or said while he was in the room.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: He asked who -- is Baranjek's wife here. I responded. He looked at me and went out. Actually, before that, he asked me, "Where is your husband?" And I replied, "You saw him in the gym."

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And were any women taken out of the gym -- sorry, of the classroom.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. Quite a few women were taken out for questioning in another classroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: When they returned, how did they look when they returned?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did they call the women out by pointing at them, or did they call them out by name?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: They called them out by name because they had a list.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Were you able to see the list?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the list when I was standing by the door and talking to the guard. My first and last name were crossed out with a red marker. I wasn't taken out for questioning at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Now, did you see Hadzic at any other point during your time in the elementary school?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him two or three more times when he was passing through the corridor and entering the classroom where the questioning was taking place. I was asking to be let out, and the guard who was guarding our classroom let me and another woman out to have a cigarette in front of the door there, and that was when I saw Hadzic pass by. I heard him yell at his people, telling them to do their job, and I don't know what else he was shouting about. At any rate, he was shouting at them, at his own people.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: What led you to conclude that they were his own people?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Because everybody was obeying him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And other than what you saw, is there anything else that you heard from the women with you about Hadzic's actions or what he said that night?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. There was a grandmother, an elderly woman who was sitting in the corridor. She said that -- in fact, all of us heard moans coming from that room. But the grandma there was an eye-witness to all that happened out there. We didn't spend that much time in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: What did she tell you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: She told me about my husband. When he was being questioned in that room. I saw him pass by because I was still in the corridor at the time. He got into that classroom. Afterwards, the grandma said he was carried out of that room in a bloody blanket.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: You said that you left the school the day after you arrived, on November 20th. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: They asked us if anybody had anyone in Serbia, in Vojvodina. I said that I had my mother's family there in Vojvodina, in Odzaci. Several among the women there, including myself, said that they would be going there. They told us to wait. It was the young man who was guarding us in that room who told us that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did you -- when you left the school, did you -- were you indeed taken to Odzaci in Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. We were taken there. I got off the bus, but I didn't go where we were supposed to be going. It was some sort of the collection centre. Together with my children and a friend, a girlfriend of mine, we went further down that road, went to a pastry shop, sat there for a while, and then continued the journey on our own.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Who was in charge of the buses that brought you there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: A man in a camouflage uniform took us out of the school. He escorted us to the bus. He told the driver -- in fact, they had stuck a paper, a Red Cross paper, onto the bus. He was armed. I don't know him. He got on the bus with us and journeyed with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Were there other -- other than this guard, were there men on the bus?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Can you repeat your question? I didn't understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: You travelled on the bus with some of the other women in the classroom. And were there also any men on the bus?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No. There was just the driver and the armed man wearing a camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And you said earlier after you got off the bus you continued the journey on your own. Where did you ultimately end up?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: It was dark. My girlfriends and I got out of the bus together with the children. We headed down the road, came across a pastry shop, and stepped in. The man asked us where we were coming from. We told him. He gave us a cup of coffee. He gave milk to the children. We were waiting for a bus. But it was late. There was no bus coming. So, ultimately, a man took us there. I was going to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat the name of the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Ma'am, where was the place you were going to?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Odzak in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you returned to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No. Only after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember what year it was?

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you ever see your husband again after leaving the school in Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And did you fill out a missing person form with the ICRC in relation to your husband?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Would you like to pause for a few moments, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I would ask that the Court Officer to please display 65 ter 3390, which is tab 2. And, Ms. Baranjek, I direct your attention to the monitor. And if you do want to take a break at any point, just let us know. But we are almost finished my questions. So is this -- do you recognise this to be the questionnaire that you filled out?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise, I don't see too well now because I left my glasses in the other room, but that's the form.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And can we now have page 3. And if we can just zoom in, then, on the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: It says on the bottom that the last information is that your husband was killed by a man who is named here as Braca Zivanovic. And I wanted to ask whether that is correct information as far as what you know today?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No. That was the statement I gave after I'd just arrived in Zagreb. But that was not the man.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: How did you -- what made you write this man down at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: He resembled the policeman who was beating him. And my girlfriend then told me that that was his name. However, later on, I found out that it was not the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person who was beating him?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No. I don't know it today.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 3390 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit P1080. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Did you subsequently hear anything else? Do you have any other information about what happened to your husband?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: I don't have any information. There were many stories rumoured, many things happened, but I haven't heard anything, haven't found out anything to this day, and not a single bone has been found.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: And what has -- can you describe the impact that his disappearance has had on you and your daughters.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: It is very hard. Ivana Fransiska was very young. She doesn't remember anything. Tamara remembers some details like seeing dead bodies along the way as we were passing by, how her father was being beaten, and some other details. I, of course, remember a bit more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: Thank you for providing your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. FRIEDMAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this time, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Baranjek, I would like to ask you one follow-up question. You told us that Mr. Hadzic, I think, at three different moments - in the gym, in the classroom, in the room where the radio transmitters were - asked for your husband, where he was. Do you know why he was particularly looking for your husband? Did he ever say something to that effect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't know why he was looking for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Christopher Gosnell. I represent Mr. Hadzic here in these proceedings. I'm going to have a few questions for you today and probably tomorrow morning as well. If anything I ask you is not clear, you don't understand, please free to ask me for clarification. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Am I right in understanding, ma'am, that you have given two different statements regarding the events that you've described here today. One statement, as I understand it, you gave in May of 2000 to some Croatian police investigators; and then, again, in 2012, on the 26th and 27th of July, you then gave a follow-up statement to an investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And could we have, please, 65 ter 03389 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you recognise that this is the statement that you gave to the Croatian police?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we could go down to the last page, the end of the document, please. Am I correct, ma'am, that that is your signature there above where it says "report submitted by," and then it says your name?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And before you did sign it, did you have an opportunity to read it in full?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you explain how that worked, that you signed it but you didn't have a chance to review it?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Because there were more of us giving statements. The police was there with us. Mistakes happened. A record is -- was made of something that didn't happen to me. It was something that I had heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I -- I -- I'm not sure I understand. Things you heard but, nevertheless, you reported accurately to the police what you had heard during your interview with the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. It was written in such a way as -- that it appeared that those were my words explaining what had happened to me; whereas, it was something that I had heard happened to others, and, as such, it wasn't valid before a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, perhaps we can -- to cut this matter short or to get beyond this, we could have a look at 05961; 65 ter 05961. And this, ma'am, coming up on the screen in front of you is your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in July 2012. Now, during that discussion with the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor, did you then have the opportunity to go through your police statement from the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. And those things were mentioned. I mean, actually, the translation wasn't good either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What do you mean, "the translation wasn't good either"?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Well, when they read it out to me, it wasn't good. Because sports hall and gym is not one and the same thing, "sportska dvorana" and "teretana," and that's what was written in the statement, and then I said so, and then that had to be corrected. And then it also had to be corrected, I mean, the thing about the policeman or the member of the milicija, whatever, his name, I mentioned that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, could we have page 5, please, of this in the English, and ... Could be page 5, could be the last page -- should be the second-last page in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, you say here you signed the document. That is your signature, is it not?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you say: "This statement has been read over to me in the Croatian language and it is true to the best of my knowledge and recollection." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. Once the things that were not written down properly were corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you had a full opportunity to review your statement from 2000 and the corrections that you wished to make in July 2012, you made in this statement, in 2012; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please go back now to 03389.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, ma'am, what I'd like to do with you is just walk through the sequence of events and touch on a few details that the Prosecution did not touch upon. And if we go over to paragraph 5 of this statement which is from 2000. As I understand the sequence of events that you describe here, you say that on the 19th of November, at around 1630 hours, as you've said here today, you left the Borovo komerc building, and then it was at about 1930 hours that you set off on foot towards what's called Mali Raj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: I don't know what time it was. It was already dark, but I thought approximately that it was about two hours that we walked.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then you arrive there at this place called Mali Raj, and there's an important sentence here. It says: "On this occasion" -- Let me go back two sentences. You have a sentence that says: "I stood by the third bus," and, ma'am, you've described today that indeed you did get on the third bus, "and at that moment my husband Ivan came up. The investigator who had searched Ivan's house in --"

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "-- in 1971 was hitting the side of the bus with his truncheon, baton." Let me just stop there. That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you say: "On this occasion, that is on 19 November, 1991, the same man was about 40 to 55 -- 45 to 50 years old wearing a military police uniform, olive-drab in colour, with a white belt and shoulder strap and a grey police cap with a star." Is that all correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this individual whom you describe here, when you say the same man, is it correct that this man had come and harassed your husband some 20 years earlier?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. He was an investigator at the then-milicija.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And just to jump ahead out of the sequence of events, you remember that you then go to the Borovo Selo elementary school. You got off the buses, and you described seeing a policeman there. Is it correct that that policeman is the same man whom you describe here as wearing the white belt?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. He was at the head of the column in that Pinzgauer and he met us at the bus door, and he started beating my husband straight away. And my husband was holding a six-month-old child at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we can turn the page in the English, please. Down towards the end of paragraph 5. You say here that: "At 2030 hours, our bus stopped outside the elementary school, so that the entrance was on our right." And then down at paragraph 6 you say: "After I had taken the child, the investigator began hitting Ivan on the kidneys with his truncheon and shouting, 'Fucking bastard. I have been waiting since 1971 to do this.'" Is that the event that you were describing, where the investigator beats your husband?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then after this event, if we go down to paragraph 7 - and I'm terribly sorry, madam, to have to go through this sequence of events with you, it says that you entered the -- the school foyer, and today you have used the word "hallway," I think. Are the hallway and the foyer one and the same place?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: The hallway, the entrance into a school, whatever you call it. I don't know. It's a biggish area. It's in a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what you say here in this statement is that there were tables set up and they told you that they were looking for weapons. Let's just stop there. Do you remember that that's what happened when you went into the hallway, that they told you that they were looking for weapons?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But instead of taking weapons, they -- they took your jewellery.

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. Everything that was valuable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then you say here in paragraph 7 of your statement at about 2100 to 2115 hours, you were taken down from the foyer by a woman with reddish curly hair to the cellar. Do you remember that detail that you were taken from the hallway down to the cellar?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. Just that woman. Her name is Senija.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And earlier today when you were describing a room where there were radio sets, is it correct that ... I'm sorry, could you repeat the name that you just mentioned. Senija, Senija. Her husband's name is Braco and they had a restaurant called Carda. They knew my mother, both she and her husband, and I recognised her when I came to the village, but she did not recognise me because I was very little when she came to my mother's.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we turn the page, please, of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you, first of all, did you consider it curious that radio sets had been set up underground presumably where they might not receive the best might -- they might not have the best transmission or reception?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: It is not underground. It is just three or four steps from the hallway. It's not a cellar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, this may be one of those translation issues. The statement from the year 2000 says that it was a cellar. But you're saying it wasn't a cellar?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. It was not a cellar. Because this room is just three or four steps lower than the hallway, whatever you call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can I ask you, when you gave your statement in the year 2000 to the Croatian police, was there anyone in particular that they were interested in? Was there any person who they had in mind as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes. They were showing me people's photographs, photographs of persons that I saw at the school in Borovo Selo, but actually I didn't know them personally. But it was there that I heard their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was Goran Hadzic one of the individuals in whom they were interested?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did they mention his name first during your interview with them, or did you mention his naming first?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No. After my statement, they showed the photographs. They weren't looking for him first. After they took my statement, then they showed us pictures, asking who knew who. Who was at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did -- did they show you a picture and say, That's Goran Hadzic. Do you recognise him? Is that how it went?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: No. No, they showed us photographs, and they asked, "Who is this man?," "Who is that man?," "Who is this man?," and then I said who it was that I recognised. I'd say the name and surname. And if I did not know a person, then I'd say that is such and such a person, but I heard at the school that this was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if you had something to say about any of these suspects, including Goran Hadzic, this was information that they were very interested in; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that? I did not quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: They were very interested in any information you might have had about Mr. Hadzic; correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, they were interested in everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And once you gave an indication that you had information about a particular person, including Mr. Hadzic, they would press you for all the information that you knew about that person; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: I would like to note that before I looked at the photographs and before they asked me about anybody, I gave a statement as to what it was that happened to me at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, all I'm asking is, once you did mention Mr. Hadzic and his activities, if they were confused, if they weren't clear, did they seek further clarification from you about what you knew about Mr. Hadzic's activities?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Again, I'm telling you, no one asked me about any details. First they took my statement on what had happened to me at the school. Then they showed me pictures of persons. And then we were supposed to say what their names were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What you say here in this statement from 2000 to the police is, and I quote in paragraph 7: "At the time we were being registered, Goran Hadzic strutted into the room wearing camouflage uniform with an unbuttoned shirt with no rank or cap and approached a radio set and contacted Novi Sad, as far as I could hear, but the only thing I heard clearly was his words: 'We'll speak later. It's all right.'"

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, that was at the very beginning when he came in. Then he called again and then he was laughing and saying, "Belgrade, Belgrade, Mladjo, send reservist. Vukovar has fallen. I can go on to Osijek tomorrow." Those are his words that I heard because this is a small room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you would have heard those words clearly because he was shouting, correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And yet you say here in your 2000 statement that the only thing I heard clearly was his words, "We'll speak later. It's all right." Why didn't you include the other words that you say now that you heard clearly?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know why it wasn't written down then. I don't know. Because I spent half an hour in that room, and he was in that room for about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: He was this in that room for ten minutes. You heard him -- apparently now you say he had two conversations, one with Belgrade, one with Novi Sad. You say now that he said the forces should push towards Osijek. And this was all in the context of an investigation by Croatian police into Goran Hadzic, and you're saying that they simply omitted these details from your statement in 2000?

utterances.speaker: SAMIRA BARANJEK
utterances.text: I don't know against whom an investigation was being carried out, and I wasn't interested in that at all. I went to the Red Cross to look for my husband, and I wasn't looking at who had been convicted and who they were looking for and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I see the time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell. Madam Witness, we finish at 2.00 for the day. Your testimony is it not ended yet. You will come back tomorrow at 9.00. You're still under oath, which means that you cannot discuss your testimony with anybody, and you cannot talk at all with any of the parties. Do you understand? Thank you. The court usher will escort you out the court now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 8th day of February, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.01 p.m.,
